title: Abulghazi (8 Sons of Japheth, Turks, Mongols, Uzbeks, Kazakhs, Mughals), Seljuks, Ottomans & Manchu/Qing China

nodes.name: Abulghazi's 8 Sons of Japheth: Turk, Chars (Khazars), Sacklap (Slavs), Russ (Russians), Maninach, Zwin (China), Camari (Gomer) & Tarich (Tiras)
nodes.role: Japhethic Progenitors of Turks, Khazars, Slavs, Russians, China & Steppe Nations
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks p. 62
nodes.notes: Abulghazi explicitly names eight sons of Japheth (Japhis) sent northward across Eurasia after Noah's Flood: 1. Turk (Japhis-Oglany), 2. Chars (Khazars), 3. Sacklap (Slavs), 4. Russ (Russians), 5. Maninach, 6. Zwin (Chin / Chinese), 7. Camari (Gomer / Cimmerians), and 8. Tarich (Tiras).

nodes.name: Turk (Japhis-Oglany) → Taunak → Ilchi → Dib Bakuy → Kayuk → Alanja Khan
nodes.role: Patrilineal Descent from Japheth's Eldest Son Turk to Alanja Khan
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks pp. 62-66
nodes.notes: Turk (Japhis-Oglany, founder of laws and tents near Issyk-Kul) fathered four sons — Taunak, Zakale, Bersazar, and Amlak — continuing from Taunak through Ilchi Khan, Dib Bakuy Khan, and Kayuk Khan to Alanja Khan.

nodes.name: Twin Sons of Alanja: Tatar Khan (7 Gens → Siuntz) & Mogul (Mung'l) Khan → Kara Khan
nodes.role: Twin Progenitors of the Tatar and Mongol Branches
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks pp. 66-69
nodes.notes: Alanja Khan divided his dominions between his twin sons: Tatar Khan (whose seven-generation line ran Bucha -> Jalanza -> Ettela -> Attaisir -> Orda -> Baydu -> Siuntz) and Mogul (Mung'l) Khan (father of Cara/Kara, Auwas, Cauwas, and Cavar).

nodes.name: Oghuz Khan's Monotheistic Restoration & Steppe Nations (Uighurs, Kanglis, Kipchaks, Karluks & 24 Oghuz Tribes)
nodes.role: Unifier of the Steppe, Conqueror of Kitay & Khorasan, Ancestor of the 24 Oghuz Tribes
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks pp. 69-82
nodes.notes: Oghuz Khan restored the worship of one God against his father Kara Khan and his Tatar kinsmen, conquering Tangut, Kitay (China), and Khorasan (Iran) following the death of Gayomart. His six sons (Buzuk Golden Bow: Kun, Ay, Yildiz; Uch-Ok Three Arrows: Kuk, Tag, Tengiz) sired the 24 Oghuz tribes alongside the Uighurs, Kanglis, Kipchaks, and Karluks.

nodes.name: Il Khan → Qiyan & Nukuz (Ergenekon / Irgana-kon) → Bertezena (Börte Čino) → Alan Qo'a → Dutumin → Kaidu → Tumana → Kabul → Bortan → Yesugei
nodes.era: Ergenekon Refuge to 12th c. CE (Abulghazi pp. 82-120)
nodes.role: Restoration from the Ergenekon Valley to the Borjigin Forefathers of Genghis Khan
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks pp. 82-120
nodes.notes: After the defeat of Il Khan, survivors Qiyan and Nukuz took refuge in the enclosed valley of Ergenekon (Irgana-kon) for generations until Bertezena (Börte Čino) led the Mongols back out onto the steppe, continuing through Alan Qo'a, Dutumin, Kaidu, Tumana, Kabul, Bortan, and Yesugei.

nodes.name: Seljuk Empire: Seljuk → Mikail → Tughril Beg (Tangrolipix, 1030) → Alp Arslan → Malik Shah → Kilij Arslan
nodes.era: 11th–12th c. CE (Knolles Vol. 1 pp. 2-15; Mod. Univ. Hist. Vol. 2)
nodes.role: Oghuz-Seljuk Sultans of Persia, Baghdad & Anatolia
sources: Knolles & Rycaut The Turkish History Vol. 1 pp. 2-15
Modern Universal History Vol. 2
Abulghazi Shajara-i Turk
nodes.notes: Knolles traces the Turks from Scythia (Tanais/Caucasus, Magog horizon) into Turcomania and Armenia, rising under Seljuk and Mikail to Tughril Beg (Tangrolipix, crowned in Persia c. 1030), Alp Arslan, Malik Shah, and the Seljuks of Rum under Kilij Arslan.

nodes.name: Ottoman Founders: Süleyman Shah → Ertuğrul → Sultan Osman I (1299) → Orhan → Murad I → Bayezid I
nodes.role: Kayi-Oghuz Founders of the Ottoman Dynasty
sources: Knolles & Rycaut The Turkish History Vol. 1
nodes.notes: Ascending from the Oghuz Kayi branch in the wake of the Seljuk disintegration, Süleyman Shah and Ertuğrul settled in Bithynia, where Osman I proclaimed sovereign rule in 1299 CE and was succeeded by Orhan, Murad I, and Bayezid I.

nodes.name: Imperial Ottomans: Mehmed II the Conqueror (1453) → Bayezid II → Selim I → Suleiman the Magnificent (1520–1566)
nodes.role: Ottoman Sultans from the Conquest of Constantinople to Imperial Zenith
sources: Knolles & Rycaut The Turkish History Vols. 1-3
nodes.notes: Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453 (ending the Byzantine Palaiologos line), followed by Bayezid II, Selim I (adding Egypt and the Hejaz), and Suleiman the Magnificent.

nodes.name: Jochi (Zuzi Chan) → Batu Sagin Chan (Golden Horde) & Berke (Burga) Khan
nodes.role: Ulus of Jochi & Rulers of the Kipchak Steppe / Golden Horde
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks Part V
nodes.notes: Abulghazi details the lineage of Genghis Khan's eldest son Jochi (Zuzi Chan) into the Golden Horde under Batu Sagin Chan and Berke (Burga) Khan across the Kipchak Steppe and Volga.

nodes.name: Shaybanid Uzbeks of Bukhara & Khwarazm: Shaybani Khan → Muhammad Shaybani (Shah Bakht) → Ilbars → Abulghazi Bahadur Khan (1603–1663)
nodes.role: Genghisid Shaybanid Khans of Bukhara & Khwarazm (Author's Own Royal Pedigree)
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks Parts VII-IX
nodes.notes: Through Jochi's fifth son Shaybani Khan, Abulghazi traces the Uzbek khans — including Muhammad Shaybani (Shah Bakht) and Ilbars Khan of Khwarazm — directly down to himself, Khan of Khiva and chronicler of the Shajara-i Turk (1603-1663).

nodes.name: Togai Timur → Crimean Khans (Caffa & Crim) & Kazakh Khans (Janibek Khan → Kasim Khan)
nodes.role: Tuka-Timurid Lines of Jochi Ruling Crimea & the Kazakh Steppe
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks pp. 252-259
nodes.notes: Abulghazi chronicles Jochi's son Togai Timur as progenitor both of the Crimean Khans (Caffa and Crim) and of the Kazakh Khans led by Janibek Khan and Kasim Khan.

nodes.name: Chagatai Khanate & Timurids: Buga Timur → Tarmashirin; Amir Timur (Tamerlane, 1370) → Shah Rukh → Ulugh Beg
nodes.era: 13th–15th c. CE (Abulghazi p. 12; Mod. Univ. Hist. Vol. 3)
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks p. 12
Modern Universal History Vol. 3
nodes.notes: Traces the house of Chagatai (Zagatai Chan) in Transoxiana and Kashgar through Buga Timur and Tarmashirin, alongside Barlas conqueror Amir Timur (Tamerlane, son-in-law/Guregen of the Chagatayids) -> Shah Rukh -> astronomer-king Ulugh Beg at Samarkand.

nodes.name: Mughal Empire of Hindustan: Zahir-ud-din Babur (1526, Timurid-Genghisid Line) → Emperor Humayun
nodes.era: 1526–1556 CE (Abulghazi p. 296; Mod. Univ. Hist. Vol. 3)
nodes.role: Founders of the Mughal Empire in Northern India
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks p. 296
Modern Universal History Vol. 3
nodes.notes: Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur — descended paternally from Timur and maternally from Genghis Khan via Chagatai — established the Mughal Empire in India in 1526 and was succeeded by Emperor Humayun.

nodes.name: Great Mughals of Delhi & Agra: Akbar the Great → Jahangir → Shah Jahan → Aurangzeb
sources: Modern Universal History Vol. 3 (History of Hindustan)
nodes.notes: Continuous Mughal imperial succession in Modern Universal History Vol. 3 from Akbar the Great through Jahangir, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb.

nodes.name: Ilkhanate of Persia: Tolui → Hulagu (Halaku) Khan (1256) → Abaqa → Ghazan Khan
nodes.era: 1256–1304 CE (Abulghazi p. 240; Mod. Univ. Hist. Vol. 2)
sources: Abulghazi Bahadur Khan General History of the Turks p. 240
Modern Universal History Vol. 2
nodes.notes: Tolui's son Hulagu (Halaku) Khan founded the Ilkhanate across Persia and Iraq in 1256, continuing through Abaqa Khan and Islamizing reformer Ghazan Khan.

nodes.name: Manchu / Qing Tartar Unification of China, Tartary, Korea & Tibet: Nurhaci (Tianming) → Hong Taiji (Tsong-te) → Shunzhi (1644) → Kangxi Emperor
nodes.era: 1616–1722 CE (Du Halde 1738 Vol. 1 Preface & p. 239; Compleat Universal History)
nodes.role: Qing Dynasty Uniting China Proper, Great Tartary, Korea & Tibet
sources: Jean-Baptiste Du Halde Description of China and Chinese-Tartary (1738 Vol. 1 Preface & p. 239)
A Compleat Universal History (China & Tartary)
Modern Universal History Vol. 5
nodes.notes: Du Halde (1738 Vol. 1 Preface & p. 239) and A Compleat Universal History document the Ming-to-Qing transition under Jurchen/Manchu Tartar founders Nurhaci (Tianming) and Hong Taiji (Tsong-te) -> Shunzhi (Shun-chi, 1644) -> Kangxi (Kang-hi), uniting China, Inner/Outer Tartary, Korea, and Tibet.
